canonical_policy.name: Respect server retry guidance
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: When a dependency supplies Retry-After or equivalent rate-limit guidance, respect it where appropriate and do not retry indefinitely or aggressively.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Appropriate RetryAfter/no indefinite-aggressive retry matches. Selected-policy support condition, inbound/outbound separation and useful known delay already captured.

context_quotes:
- Retry only when repeating the operation is safe; never retry state-changing operations automatically without idempotency or another concrete duplicate-prevention mechanism.
- Default: when a dependency supplies `Retry-After` or equivalent rate-limit guidance, respect it where appropriate, and never retry indefinitely or aggressively.
- Use a fallback only when its result is semantically acceptable; never hide a correctness failure behind a convenient default value.

When a remote service returns `429 Too Many Requests`, honor `Retry-After` when the selected retry policy supports it. Outbound retry behavior and the inbound response your own API returns are separate decisions.

New `HttpClient` per request; mandating one client model everywhere; retrying unsafe operations without idempotency analysis; unbounded retries; leaking `HttpResponseMessage` across boundaries; ignoring cancellation; dynamic tokens in shared default headers; mapping every upstream failure to the same status; resilience pipelines added without understanding them.

Prefer the server's retry guidance when the policy supports it instead of an independent aggressive schedule against a rate-limited dependency.

ASP.NET Core rate limiting protects this API from excessive incoming traffic and is separate from outbound resilience; rejected requests get `429` with `Retry-After` when a useful delay is known (`http-api`).

| Scenario | Consideration |
|---|---|
| External I/O | Bounded execution time |
| Safe transient HTTP failure | Consider retry |
| Unsafe write | No retry unless duplicate-safe |
| `429` from dependency | Honor `Retry-After` where appropriate |
| Repeated dependency outage | Consider circuit breaker |
| Optional data unavailable | Consider explicit fallback |
| Latency-sensitive idempotent read | Consider hedging after measurement |
| EF transient faults | Provider/EF execution strategy |
| Incoming request rate limiting | ASP.NET Core rate limiter |
Consider rate limiting where abuse realistically matters — login and password reset, expensive anonymous endpoints, resource-intensive operations — not on every endpoint. `429` semantics: `http-api`.

canonical_policy.name: Caller cancellation is not a transient failure
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Do not classify caller cancellation as a transient dependency failure or convert it into repeated outbound attempts.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Caller cancellation not transient/retried matches; distinct own/upstream timeout and API role already0425. No new repeat-attempt exception.

context_quotes:

**504 Gateway Timeout** — acting as an intermediary, an upstream service did not respond in time. Not every internal `TaskCanceledException` is `504`: distinguish a client-cancelled request, our own operation timing out, and an upstream dependency timing out — the right response depends on which occurred and the role this API plays.

Plausibly transient failures: selected network failures, temporary unavailability, rate limiting where retry is allowed, transient provider-specific database failures. Not retried: validation errors, authentication/authorization failures, permanent `404`, deterministic business rejection, non-idempotent operations without duplicate prevention.

Propagate caller cancellation through resilience pipelines; it is not a transient failure to retry.
Review retries of state-changing operations — a lost response followed by a retry can duplicate effects — and retries triggered by caller cancellation. Technique: `httpclient-factory`.

canonical_policy.name: C# file and async naming conventions remain conventional
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: For new C# code, prefer file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the project, normally keep one primary top-level type per matching file, and use the Async suffix for Task/ValueTask-returning methods unless an existing or framework contract makes that inappropriate.

reviews.boundary_analysis: New-code namespace/type/file/Async default with contract exception matches; small private/nested exception replica0056. Async-modifier-only enforcement and missing contract exceptions alreadyBF0076. Role naming/subdirectory thresholdEXTRA0198.

context_quotes:
- Do not perform style-only rewrites outside the requested change unless explicitly asked; avoid mixing large formatting or modernization changes with functional work.
- Default for new code: file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the project; one primary top-level type per file, with the file named after it (small private or nested supporting types may stay with their owner); the `Async` suffix on `Task`/`ValueTask`-returning methods unless an existing or framework contract makes it inappropriate. Do not reorganize an existing file merely to satisfy a preferred member ordering.
- Prefer primary constructors for simple dependency injection or initialization, and a regular constructor when validation or initialization is non-trivial, explicit fields read better, or the codebase consistently uses that style; do not convert constructors mechanically.
- Prefer records where value semantics and immutability are intended (many DTOs, genuine Value Objects) and classes where identity, mutable lifecycle, inheritance or framework behavior matters; do not turn every DTO or Domain type into a record.
- Keep implementation details non-public unless they belong to the project's public API; use `sealed` when it communicates deliberate design intent, not as a speculative optimization.
- Prefer `var` when the type is obvious from the right-hand side or unimportant, and an explicit type when it aids understanding. Use standard .NET naming (PascalCase for types and members, camelCase for parameters and locals, meaningful names over abbreviations); private-field naming follows the repository's convention.

Within a feature or service area, make each supporting type's responsibility clear from its name, its directory or both. Useful suffixes:

```text
Service            use-case orchestration
Dto                data-transfer model
Request/Response   Application operation contracts (HTTP contracts belong to Api)
Result/Outcome     operation results
Validator          validation
Rules/Policy       decision or workflow rules
Factory            object creation
Mapper             mapping
Adapter            boundary adaptation
```

Prefer `TaskWorkflowRules`, `TaskWorkflowPolicy` or `TaskWorkflowService` over an ambiguous `TaskWorkflow`. Add responsibility-specific subdirectories when a flat feature directory becomes hard to navigate, not to classify one or two obvious files. Avoid generic `Models`, `Helpers`, `Common` or `Utils` buckets when a specific responsibility can be named.
